prompt.context: Your client, CavalierChem, is a global chemicals manufacturer. CavalierChem recently acquired a manufacturing facility that makes surfactants as part of a larger purchase of competitor assets. Surfactants are a specialty chemical used for a variety of purposes, including laundry detergent, and the client has very little prior experience with this type of product. The manufacturing facility is not currently generating profits, and the client wants your help in determining what to do.
prompt.question: What should CavalierChem do with the surfactant manufacturing facility?

clarifying_info.q: Does CavalierChem have a target in mind?
clarifying_info.a: The client wants to make the highest return from this facility as possible in the next 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is CavalierChem's core business / how do they make money?
clarifying_info.a: 80% of CavalierChem's revenues come from the sale of commodity plastics to other manufacturers. The other 20% comes from a wide mix of products that are either downstream or byproducts of their core business.

clarifying_info.q: Why did they make this acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: The manufacturing facility in question was part of a bundled acquisition of other manufacturing assets that are of strategic importance to CavalierChem. CavalierChem now wants to evaluate the surfactant factory on its own.

clarifying_info.q: What does the surfactant market look like?
clarifying_info.a: The market for this particular surfactant is $300M annually. CavalierChem and one other competitor are the only significant manufacturers.

exhibits.title: Average cost and profit breakdown for surfactants in cents/lb
exhibits.shows: Bar chart comparing CavalierChem and its competitor across three cost/profit components (Variable Cost, Fixed Cost, Profit) measured in cents per pound.

framework: Increase Profitability: analyze revenues (price, contracts, market share) and costs (variable: COGS, hourly labor, utilities; fixed: overhead, maintenance, salaried, SG&A)
Repurpose: identify products with similar manufacturing processes, evaluate those markets, estimate CapEx/OpEx and timeline
Divest: assess potential sale price, consider monopoly risk for competition, effects on customer relationships and employees

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 1 tell you about CavalierChem's prospects for raising profits?
questions.guidance: Candidate should notice that variable costs and fixed costs are identical between CavalierChem and the competitor (2.3 and 2.7 cents/lb respectively), but the competitor earns 4x the profit (2.0 vs 0.5 cents/lb). Since costs are the same, the key lever is on the revenue (pricing) side. Candidate should ask about sales structure and pricing to investigate the gap.

math.setup: CavalierChem sells 1.4 million tons/year; 75% on contract, 25% on spot market. CavalierChem contract price = 5.67 cents/lb; Competitor contract price = 7.67 cents/lb; Spot price (both) = 5 cents/lb. Calculate incremental profit from matching competitor contract price.
steps: 1.4 million tons * 2,000 lbs/ton = 2.8 billion lbs total annual volume
2.8 billion lbs * 75% on contract = 2.1 billion lbs sold on contract
4.2 billion cents / 100 = $42 million incremental annual profit
Over 5 years (no discount): $42M * 5 = $210M total cash flow

questions.prompt: How are some ways CavalierChem can raise its per-pound price? (Brainstorm)
questions.guidance: Strong candidates structure their ideas into customer-focused and product-focused buckets. Great candidates also circle back to the other strategic options (repurpose or divest) after the brainstorm.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the repurpose and divest options: which path generates the most cash over 5 years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recall the 5-year horizon from clarifying info and ignore discount rate unless asked. Compare the three options on total 5-year cash flows.

math.setup: Renegotiate contracts: $42M/year * 5 years = $210M. Repurpose: $50M CapEx upfront, $75M incremental annual profit, starts generating in year 3 (2-year start-up). Divest: one-time sale price of $200M.
math.answer: Renegotiate contracts: $210M; Repurpose: $175M; Divest: $200M. Renegotiate generates the highest 5-year cash flow.

brainstorming.prompt: Now that we know our revenues are below those of our competitors, what are some ways we can raise that per-pound price?

categories.name: Customer focused
ideas: Change sales mix of contract vs spot
Change sales mix to emphasize highest-paying customers
Develop strong relationships with top-paying customers (sales dinners, events, etc.)
Renegotiate existing contracts to higher prices
Increase advertising to develop a premium brand

categories.name: Product focused
ideas: Make production process more sustainable and charge a green premium
Modify product to reduce customer use costs and capture part of their savings

recommendation: CavalierChem should renegotiate contract prices to match the competition at 7.67 cents/lb
This will grow annual profits by $42M, generating $210M over 5 years — the highest of the three options evaluated
risks: Some customers may not be able to afford higher prices and could reduce orders or churn
The market may contract if prices rise, reducing total volume
All three options (renegotiate, repurpose, divest) have roughly equivalent NPVs at a 10% discount rate, so the choice depends on strategic fit
next_steps: Analyze customers' cost structures to assess willingness and ability to pay higher prices
Solicit alternative bids for the asset sale to validate the $200M divestiture price
Evaluate repurposing timeline and CapEx commitments in more detail before ruling it out
